title: Person-centred — grief (session 6)

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Where would you like to start today?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I'm not sure. It's been six months since Mum died and people keep saying I should be feeling better by now.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: There's a sense that other people have a timetable for your grief.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yes. My brother especially. He's back to normal, he says. And I'm still crying in the supermarket when I see her biscuits.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Her biscuits.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: The ones she always bought. Custard creams. Stupid, really.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: It doesn't sound stupid. It sounds like small things carry a lot of her.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: They do. Everything does. Her coat is still in my hall.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I can't move it. My brother says I should give her things to charity.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Part of you isn't ready to let her coat go.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: If I move it, it's like she's really gone.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Keeping it there keeps something of her close.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yes. I talk to it sometimes. Isn't that mad?

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: You're wondering whether I'll think it's mad.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: A bit, yes.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: I don't. It sounds like a way of staying connected to her.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: That's a relief to hear, actually.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I suppose I'm also angry. With my brother. And with her, for not going to the doctor sooner.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Angry with her too.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Which makes me feel terrible. She's dead and I'm angry at her.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: It's hard to let yourself feel angry with someone you love and miss so much.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yes. I've never said that out loud before.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: You've said it here.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I have. It feels a bit lighter, weirdly.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: We're coming towards the end of our time. How are you leaving today?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Tired, but okay. I think I want to talk more about the anger next week.

expected_note_facts: Six months since client's mother died
Client feels pressure from others (especially brother) to be 'better'
Client cries when seeing reminders, e.g. mother's biscuits
Mother's coat still in client's hall; client not ready to move it; talks to it
Client expressed anger with brother and with mother for not seeing doctor sooner; first time saying this aloud
Client wishes to explore anger next session

strengths: Stayed with the client's frame ('Her biscuits')
Named the client's fear of judgement and responded with acceptance
Made space for anger without rushing to reassure
missed_openings: The relationship with the brother and feeling out of step with him could be explored
Feeling 'lighter' after naming anger could have been reflected further
try_next: Allow a little more silence after significant disclosures

review: CLINICAL-REVIEW: synthetic role-play; drafts for the Clinical Lead.
